solution: The denominators ${=p}$ and ${=q}$ have no common factor, so the lowest common denominator is ${=p}\times {=q}={=p*q}$.

Write each fraction over ${=p*q}$ by multiplying its numerator and its denominator by the missing factor: the first fraction by ${=q}$ and the second by ${=p}$. $\dfrac{x+{=a}}{{=p}}+\dfrac{x+{=b}}{{=q}}=\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})}{{=p*q}}+\dfrac{{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}$

Put both numerators over the one common denominator and remove the brackets, multiplying every term inside each bracket. $\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})}{{=p*q}}+\dfrac{{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})+{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=q}x+{=q*a}+{=p}x+{=p*b}}{{=p*q}}$
Collect the like terms in the numerator. $\dfrac{{=q}x+{=q*a}+{=p}x+{=p*b}}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=p+q}x+{=q*a+p*b}}{{=p*q}}$

This cannot be simplified further, because the coefficient ${=p+q}$ of $x$ and the denominator ${=p*q}$ have no common factor. So $\dfrac{x+{=a}}{{=p}}+\dfrac{x+{=b}}{{=q}}=\dfrac{{=p+q}x+{=q*a+p*b}}{{=p*q}}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Multiplies only the first term of the numerator by the missing factor
proposed_misconceptions.description: When rewriting a fraction over the lowest common denominator, the student multiplies the denominator and the x-term of the numerator by the missing factor but leaves the constant term as it was, as if the factor were not applied to the whole bracket.

notes: Basic = the entry point of the skill: add two fractions whose denominators are different small numbers with no common factor (so the LCD is their product), each numerator a linear x + constant, all signs positive. This is the book's own method from ex1-10-3a / ex1-10-2q (LCD, multiply each numerator through, remove brackets, collect like terms) minus the subtraction sign hazard, which stays with the standard-tier book questions; addition of two fractions over their LCD is also what ex1-10-3d and 3f do. Parameters: p in 2..5, q in 2..7, coprime (15 denominator pairs), a and b in 1..6 and different (30 pairs), so 450 instances. Every instance is clean: p+q >= 5 so the x coefficient is never 1 (no '1x' rendering), and gcd(p+q, p*q) = 1 whenever gcd(p, q) = 1, so the final fraction is always in lowest terms and the last solution step is true for every instance. The four options are always pairwise distinct: the correct numerator has x-coefficient p+q >= 5 and constant q*a+p*b, D1 has coefficient 2 and denominator p+q (never equal to p*q for coprime p, q >= 2), D2 has coefficient 2, D3 has the right coefficient but constant a+b, which differs from q*a+p*b because (q-1)*a+(p-1)*b > 0. Distractors: D1 adds numerators and adds denominators (catalogued mc adds-numerators-and-denominators-separately); D2 writes the common denominator p*q but leaves both numerators unscaled, so the x terms add to 2x (catalogued mc numerator-or-whole-number-not-scaled); D3 scales only the x term of each numerator and not the constant, one new misconception declared here. The catalogued mc sign-changed-on-first-term-only needs a subtraction and is not used on this addition-only basic family. mcq is used because every distractor is a specific diagnosable error, not to avoid typing; if the reviewer prefers a typed answer the correct option converts directly to an expression marker.
